Chapter 11. The Politics of Memory: Whose Story Gets Told?
As time moved on, questions about memory took on a new urgency. Think about it—whose story actually gets remembered? Whose pain do we choose to acknowledge? In the capital, they built grand monuments to honor those who'd fallen. But if you looked closer, those statues and plaques only shared part of the story.
Picture a group of students visiting one of these war memorials. Their teacher explains the official version of what happened. Some kids listen quietly, but others lean in, whispering stories they'd heard at home—tales that often sound very different from what’s being taught. That gap between what everyone’s supposed to remember, and what families actually talk about behind closed doors? It just keeps growing.
Meanwhile, up north, families have their own ways of remembering. They gather around simple memorials—just a stone, maybe a faded photo, and a bunch of fresh flowers. For them, memory is about more than heroes. It’s about the victims, the missing, the ones nobody talks about. In these small acts, remembering becomes a quiet form of resistance—a way to make sure the truth doesn’t disappear.
The government, on the other hand, keeps pushing a message of unity and reconciliation. They want everyone to focus on moving forward. But for so many people, that message feels like it’s missing something, leaving out the pain and the complexity of lives shaped by loss and survival.
That’s where writers, artists, and activists step in. They create poems, paint murals, and put on plays—trying to fill in the blanks, to show the parts of the story that the official version leaves out. Some get applause, while others are silenced. The fight over memory isn’t just about what happened in the past. It’s about who gets to decide the future—who shapes the identity of the country itself.
So, here’s something to really pay attention to: memory is political. The stories we tell—and the ones we’re told to forget—are going to shape the island for generations. Which stories will last? And whose voices will finally be heard?
